questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agriculture can be broadly defined as the
options: process of extracting minerals from the earth
deliberate cultivation of crops and rearing of animals for human use
manufacturing of industrial machinery
study of wild plants in their natural habitat
questions.explanation: Agriculture encompasses the purposeful growing of crops and raising of livestock to provide food, fibre, and other products for human needs.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a branch of agriculture concerned specifically with the study of soil?
options: Animal husbandry
Agricultural economics
Pedology (soil science)
Agronomy
questions.explanation: Pedology, or soil science, specifically studies soil formation, classification, and properties, distinct from agronomy (crop production) and animal husbandry.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Subsistence farming is best described as farming carried out mainly to
options: export produce to other countries
generate maximum profit through large-scale sale of produce
produce food for the farmer's family with little or no surplus for sale
supply raw materials to large industries
questions.explanation: Subsistence farming is small-scale, aimed at feeding the farming household, unlike commercial farming, which is large-scale and profit-driven.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Commercial farming differs from subsistence farming mainly in that commercial farming is carried out
options: on a small scale, mainly to feed the farmer's household
on a large scale, primarily for profit and sale of produce
without the use of modern machinery
only for the cultivation of food crops
questions.explanation: Commercial farming is characterised by large-scale production, mechanisation, and market-oriented output, distinguishing it from small-scale subsistence farming.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agriculture contributes to the Nigerian economy mainly by
options: being the sole source of the country's electricity
providing food, raw materials for industry, employment, and foreign exchange earnings
serving only as a source of government tax revenue
replacing the need for a manufacturing sector entirely
questions.explanation: Agriculture supports the economy through food security, supplying raw materials (e.g., cotton, cocoa) to industries, generating employment, and earning foreign exchange through exports.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following best describes agronomy as a branch of agriculture?
options: The economics of farm business
The study and management of livestock
The science of crop production and soil management
The engineering of farm machinery
questions.explanation: Agronomy focuses specifically on crop cultivation practices and the management of soils to optimise crop yield and quality.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which branch of agriculture deals with the breeding, feeding, and management of farm animals?
options: Agronomy
Forestry
Horticulture
Animal husbandry
questions.explanation: Animal husbandry (livestock production) covers the practical aspects of raising farm animals, including breeding, nutrition, housing, and health management.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Horticulture is a branch of agriculture concerned with the cultivation of
options: cereal crops only
fruits, vegetables, and ornamental plants
forest trees for timber
livestock for meat production
questions.explanation: Horticulture specifically deals with intensively cultivated plants such as fruits, vegetables, flowers, and ornamentals, as distinct from broad-acre agronomy.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agricultural extension services are primarily aimed at
options: regulating international agricultural trade
selling farm produce directly to consumers
providing loans exclusively to large-scale industrial farms
transferring improved farming knowledge and techniques from researchers to farmers
questions.explanation: Extension services bridge the gap between agricultural research institutions and farmers, disseminating new techniques and information to improve farm productivity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is an importance of agriculture to a nation's industrial development?
options: It supplies raw materials such as cotton, rubber, and palm oil to agro-based industries
It provides direct funding to build factories
It eliminates the need for any manufacturing sector
It replaces the need for import and export activities
questions.explanation: Many industries (textiles, food processing, rubber manufacturing) rely directly on agricultural raw materials, linking agriculture closely to industrial growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The rainforest ecological zone of West Africa is characterised mainly by
options: high rainfall and dense, tall evergreen vegetation
extremely short daylight hours year-round
permanently frozen ground
very low rainfall and sparse, thorny vegetation
questions.explanation: The rainforest belt receives abundant, well-distributed rainfall throughout the year, supporting tall, dense, multi-layered evergreen forest vegetation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which crop is most commonly associated with the rainforest ecological zone of Nigeria?
options: Millet
Groundnut
Cotton
Cocoa
questions.explanation: Cocoa thrives in the warm, humid conditions and high rainfall of the rainforest zone, making it a major cash crop of that region in Nigeria.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The Guinea savanna ecological zone is characterised by
options: moderate rainfall with a mix of grassland and scattered trees
the highest rainfall of all ecological zones
permanent snow cover
vegetation consisting only of mangrove swamps
questions.explanation: The Guinea savanna, occupying much of Nigeria's middle belt, has moderate rainfall supporting a mixture of tall grasses and scattered deciduous trees.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which crop is predominantly cultivated in the Sudan and Sahel savanna zones due to their low rainfall?
options: Cocoa
Oil palm
Millet
Rubber
questions.explanation: Millet is drought-tolerant and well-suited to the low, erratic rainfall of the Sudan and Sahel savanna zones in northern Nigeria.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The mangrove swamp ecological zone is found mainly
options: in the far northern semi-arid regions
in areas with the lowest rainfall in the country
along the coastline, where fresh and salt water mix
at high elevations in mountainous areas
questions.explanation: Mangrove swamps occur in coastal areas influenced by tidal, brackish water, supporting salt-tolerant mangrove vegetation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Rainfall is a critical climatic factor in agriculture mainly because it
options: determines soil colour but not crop yield
only affects livestock and not crop production
directly determines the amount of water available for crop growth and the choice of crops grown
has no significant effect on crop distribution
questions.explanation: Rainfall amount and distribution strongly influence which crops can be successfully grown in a given ecological zone, from drought-tolerant millet to high-rainfall cocoa.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Temperature as an environmental factor affects crop and livestock production mainly by influencing
options: the political boundaries of farmland
the type of currency used in agricultural trade
the price of farm produce in the market
the rate of physiological processes such as photosynthesis, respiration, and growth
questions.explanation: Temperature directly affects metabolic and physiological processes in plants and animals, with each species having an optimal temperature range for growth and productivity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following ecological zones in West Africa generally has the lowest annual rainfall?
options: Sahel savanna
Rainforest
Mangrove swamp
Guinea savanna
questions.explanation: The Sahel savanna, bordering the Sahara Desert, receives the least rainfall among West Africa's major ecological zones, supporting sparse grass and thorny shrubs.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Light intensity and duration (photoperiod) affect crop production mainly by influencing
options: the mineral content of the soil
the breed of livestock best suited to an area
the rate of photosynthesis and the timing of flowering in some crops
the pH of rainwater
questions.explanation: Photoperiod-sensitive crops flower only when day length matches specific requirements, and light intensity directly drives the rate of photosynthesis.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Relative humidity, an important climatic factor, refers to the
options: amount of water vapour present in the air relative to the maximum it can hold at that temperature
total volume of rainfall received annually
temperature of the soil at a given depth
speed of prevailing winds in a region
questions.explanation: Relative humidity measures the air's water vapour content as a percentage of the maximum possible at a given temperature, affecting evaporation, transpiration, and disease spread.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A cutlass (machete) is classified as a
options: type of farm machinery for planting
simple hand tool used for clearing land and harvesting
irrigation device
primary tillage implement pulled by a tractor
questions.explanation: The cutlass is a basic manually operated hand tool used for tasks like clearing vegetation, weeding, and harvesting some crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The plough is primarily used in farm operations for
options: primary tillage, to break and turn over the soil
irrigating farmland
harvesting mature grain crops
spraying pesticides on crops
questions.explanation: Ploughing is the first major tillage operation, breaking up and inverting the soil to bury crop residues and prepare a suitable seedbed.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Harrowing is a secondary tillage operation carried out mainly to
options: harvest root crops
dig deep drainage channels
apply fertiliser to the soil
break up large soil clods left after ploughing and create a finer tilth
questions.explanation: Harrowing follows ploughing, further pulverising the soil into a finer, more uniform tilth suitable for planting seeds.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A tractor in modern agriculture is mainly used to
options: provide power for pulling and operating various farm implements
measure soil pH
irrigate crops directly
store harvested grains
questions.explanation: Tractors serve as the primary power source on mechanised farms, pulling ploughs, harrows, planters, and other implements to perform various operations.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A combine harvester is a machine designed to perform which combination of operations simultaneously?
options: Ploughing, harrowing, and ridging
Reaping (cutting), threshing, and cleaning of grain crops
Milking, feeding, and housing of livestock
Planting, weeding, and spraying
questions.explanation: A combine harvester combines several harvesting operations, cutting the crop, separating grain from stalks (threshing), and cleaning the grain, all in one pass.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Regular maintenance of farm machinery, such as changing engine oil and greasing moving parts, is important mainly to
options: prolong the machine's useful life and prevent breakdowns
increase the purchase cost of the machine
reduce the machine's fuel efficiency
eliminate the need for skilled operators
questions.explanation: Routine maintenance reduces wear, prevents costly breakdowns, and extends the operational lifespan of expensive farm machinery.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A hoe is a simple farm tool primarily used for
options: weeding, making ridges, and light tillage
deep ploughing of large fields
spraying chemicals over a wide area
harvesting tree crops
questions.explanation: The hoe is a versatile hand tool used for shallow cultivation tasks such as weeding, making ridges or mounds, and planting.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A ridger, whether animal-drawn or tractor-mounted, is used mainly to
options: measure the moisture content of soil
form ridges or mounds in preparation for planting certain crops
harvest cereal crops
spray insecticides on growing crops
questions.explanation: Ridging creates raised soil ridges that improve drainage and aeration, commonly used for crops like yam, cassava, and maize before planting.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is classified as a secondary tillage implement?
options: Mould-board plough
Disc plough
Harrow
Sub-soiler
questions.explanation: Primary tillage implements (mould-board plough, disc plough, sub-soiler) perform the initial deep soil-breaking, while the harrow performs secondary tillage to refine the seedbed.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Irrigation equipment such as sprinklers is used on farms mainly to
options: supply water to crops in areas or seasons with insufficient rainfall
measure the depth of the water table
harvest water-loving crops like rice
remove excess water from waterlogged fields
questions.explanation: Irrigation systems, including sprinklers, artificially supply water to crops when natural rainfall is inadequate, ensuring consistent crop growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil is formed mainly through the process of
options: photosynthesis in plants
combustion of organic matter
weathering of parent rock material over a long period
condensation of atmospheric water vapour
questions.explanation: Soil formation (pedogenesis) results from the physical, chemical, and biological weathering of parent rock, combined with the addition of organic matter over time.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The soil profile is best described as the
options: horizontal spread of soil across a farm
total weight of soil in a given area
vertical arrangement of distinct layers (horizons) from the surface down to the parent rock
chemical composition of soil water only
questions.explanation: A soil profile shows the sequence of horizons (typically topsoil, subsoil, and parent material) that develop as soil forms over time.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The topsoil (A horizon) is generally the most fertile layer of soil mainly because it
options: consists mainly of unweathered parent rock
is the layer furthest from plant roots
lacks any nutrients accessible to plants
contains the highest concentration of organic matter and living organisms
questions.explanation: Topsoil accumulates decomposed organic matter (humus) and hosts the most biological activity, making it the most fertile and productive soil layer for crop growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil texture refers to the
options: colour of the soil
relative proportion of sand, silt, and clay particles in the soil
arrangement of soil particles into aggregates
depth of the soil profile
questions.explanation: Soil texture describes the proportions of differently sized mineral particles (sand, silt, clay), which strongly influence water retention, drainage, and aeration.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil structure refers to the
options: proportion of sand and clay in the soil
chemical elements present in the soil
depth to the water table
arrangement of individual soil particles into aggregates (crumbs or clods)
questions.explanation: Soil structure describes how individual soil particles clump together into larger aggregates, affecting porosity, aeration, and root penetration.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A loamy soil, considered ideal for most crops, contains a balanced mixture of
options: only sand and gravel
only clay particles
sand, silt, and clay
only organic matter with no mineral particles
questions.explanation: Loam soils combine the drainage benefits of sand, the nutrient and water retention of clay, and the moderate properties of silt, making them ideal for most crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil water available for plant uptake, held in the small pore spaces against gravity, is called
options: gravitational water
hygroscopic water
water vapour
capillary water
questions.explanation: Capillary water is held in small soil pores by surface tension against the pull of gravity, making it the main source of water available for plant absorption.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Nitrogen, an essential plant nutrient, is important mainly for
options: vegetative growth and the formation of proteins and chlorophyll
increasing the sweetness of fruit
improving fruit colour only
strengthening cell walls only
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is a key component of amino acids, proteins, and chlorophyll, driving leafy vegetative growth in plants; deficiency causes yellowing (chlorosis) of leaves.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is an organic manure used to improve soil fertility?
options: Urea fertiliser
NPK fertiliser
Single superphosphate
Farmyard manure
questions.explanation: Farmyard manure, composed of decomposed animal dung and plant residue, is an organic source of nutrients and organic matter, unlike synthetic inorganic fertilisers like urea and NPK.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The main advantage of inorganic (chemical) fertilisers over organic manures is that inorganic fertilisers
options: improve soil structure more effectively than organic manure
are always cheaper than organic manure
supply nutrients in concentrated, readily available forms that act quickly
add significant organic matter to the soil
questions.explanation: Inorganic fertilisers provide specific nutrients in concentrated, soluble forms for rapid plant uptake, though they don't improve soil structure or add organic matter like manures do.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In the nitrogen cycle, the process by which nitrogen gas in the atmosphere is converted to ammonia by certain bacteria is called
options: nitrogen fixation
ammonification
denitrification
nitrification
questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation, carried out by bacteria such as Rhizobium (often in legume root nodules) or Azotobacter, converts inert atmospheric nitrogen into usable ammonia compounds.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Nitrification is the process by which
options: atmospheric nitrogen is fixed into ammonia
ammonia is converted into nitrites and then nitrates by soil bacteria
nitrates are converted back into atmospheric nitrogen gas
organic nitrogen compounds are broken down into ammonia
questions.explanation: Nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter) oxidise ammonia stepwise into nitrites and then nitrates, the form of nitrogen most readily absorbed by plant roots.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Denitrification, generally undesirable for soil fertility, is the process by which
options: atmospheric nitrogen is converted into ammonia
nitrites are converted into nitrates
organic matter decomposes into humus
nitrates are converted back into atmospheric nitrogen gas by certain bacteria
questions.explanation: Denitrifying bacteria, active in poorly aerated (waterlogged) soils, convert valuable nitrates back into gaseous nitrogen, which escapes to the atmosphere, reducing soil nitrogen availability.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil pH is important in agriculture mainly because it affects the
options: availability of plant nutrients in the soil
amount of rainfall an area receives
colour of the topsoil only
depth of the soil profile
questions.explanation: Soil pH strongly influences the chemical forms and solubility of nutrients, so extreme acidity or alkalinity can make essential nutrients unavailable to plants even if present in the soil.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Liming (adding calcium compounds) is a common practice used to
options: improve soil drainage in clay soils only
reduce soil acidity and raise soil pH
add nitrogen to the soil
increase soil acidity
questions.explanation: Agricultural lime neutralises excess soil acidity by supplying calcium (and often magnesium) compounds, raising pH to a range more favourable for most crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil erosion is best described as the
options: chemical weathering of parent rock
addition of organic matter to the topsoil
removal and displacement of topsoil by agents such as water and wind
compaction of soil due to heavy machinery
questions.explanation: Soil erosion occurs when the fertile topsoil is detached and carried away by erosive agents like flowing water or wind, especially on bare or poorly managed land.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Crops are broadly classified based on their use into categories such as
options: tropical crops only
annual crops only
food crops, cash crops, and fibre crops
monocotyledons only
questions.explanation: Crops can be classified by their primary use, e.g., food crops (maize, rice) for consumption, cash crops (cocoa, cotton) mainly for sale, and fibre crops (cotton, jute) for textiles.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cereal crops, such as maize, rice, and millet, belong to which plant family?
options: Solanaceae
Malvaceae
Gramineae (Poaceae)
Leguminosae (Fabaceae)
questions.explanation: Cereals are grasses belonging to the family Gramineae (also called Poaceae), characterised by narrow leaves and grain-bearing inflorescences.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Leguminous crops, such as cowpea and groundnut, are agriculturally valuable mainly because they
options: cannot be intercropped with cereals
are resistant to all pests and diseases
fix atmospheric nitrogen into the soil through root nodule bacteria
require no fertiliser of any kind
questions.explanation: Legumes host nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules, enriching the soil with nitrogen, which benefits both the legume and subsequent crops in rotation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is classified as a root and tuber crop?
options: Maize
Cotton
Cassava
Cowpea
questions.explanation: Cassava, along with yam and sweet potato, is grown for its starchy underground root or tuber, distinguishing it from cereal, legume, and fibre crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The correct order of operations in maize husbandry typically begins with
options: land preparation, followed by planting, weeding, fertiliser application, and harvesting
fertiliser application before land preparation
harvesting before land preparation
weeding before planting
questions.explanation: Proper crop husbandry follows a logical sequence: preparing the land first, then planting, followed by weeding and fertilising during growth, and finally harvesting at maturity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Crop rotation, the practice of growing different crops in succession on the same land, is beneficial mainly because it
options: eliminates the need for fertiliser permanently
guarantees the same yield every season regardless of soil condition
helps control pests/diseases and maintains soil fertility
requires no planning of what to grow next
questions.explanation: Rotating crops (e.g., alternating cereals with legumes) disrupts pest and disease cycles specific to one crop and helps balance nutrient use and replenishment in the soil.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Crop improvement through selective breeding aims mainly to develop varieties with
options: higher yield, disease resistance, and better quality
permanently fixed genetic traits that never change
no need for water or sunlight
smaller root systems for easier harvesting only
questions.explanation: Plant breeding programs select and cross parent plants to combine desirable traits such as high yield, pest/disease resistance, and improved nutritional or market quality.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Weeds are undesirable in crop fields mainly because they
options: attract only beneficial insects
add significant organic matter that boosts yield
compete with crops for nutrients, water, light, and space
improve soil structure more than crops do
questions.explanation: Weeds reduce crop yield and quality by competing directly with cultivated crops for essential growth resources like sunlight, water, and soil nutrients.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Chemical control of weeds is achieved mainly through the application of
options: fungicides
insecticides
herbicides
nematicides
questions.explanation: Herbicides are chemicals specifically formulated to kill or suppress unwanted plant growth (weeds) without excessively harming the crop.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a common method of pest control in crop production?
options: Use of insecticides
Liming the soil
Use of herbicides
Deep ploughing to bury seeds only
questions.explanation: Insecticides are chemicals specifically used to kill or control insect pests that damage crops, distinct from herbicides (for weeds) and fungicides (for fungal diseases).

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Crop diseases caused by fungi, such as blight, are typically controlled by applying
options: rodenticides
fungicides
insecticides
herbicides
questions.explanation: Fungicides are chemical agents specifically designed to prevent or eliminate fungal infections in crops, such as blights, rusts, and mildews.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a biological method of pest control?
options: Introducing natural predators or parasites of the pest
Applying synthetic herbicides
Burning the affected crop field
Spraying broad-spectrum chemical insecticides
questions.explanation: Biological control uses natural enemies (predators, parasites, or pathogens) of a pest species to reduce its population, an environmentally friendly alternative to chemical control.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Forestry, as it relates to agriculture, is primarily concerned with the
options: cultivation of only food crops
rearing of livestock in forest reserves exclusively
management and conservation of forest resources for timber and other products
processing of dairy products
questions.explanation: Forestry involves the sustainable management of trees and forest ecosystems, providing timber, fuelwood, and other products while supporting conservation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Afforestation refers to the
options: planting of trees in an area that previously had no forest cover
burning of forest vegetation for farmland
cutting down of trees in an existing forest
harvesting of mature timber trees
questions.explanation: Afforestation involves establishing new forest cover on land that was not previously forested, as opposed to deforestation, which removes existing forest.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Deforestation, the large-scale clearing of forests, commonly leads to
options: improved water retention in the soil
higher local rainfall in all cases
increased soil fertility permanently
soil erosion and loss of biodiversity
questions.explanation: Removing forest cover exposes soil to erosion by wind and rain and destroys habitats, leading to significant loss of biodiversity and long-term land degradation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following crops is classified as a fibre crop?
options: Groundnut
Cotton
Yam
Tomato
questions.explanation: Cotton is cultivated primarily for the fibre surrounding its seeds, used in the textile industry, distinguishing it from food and tuber crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Intercropping, the practice of growing two or more crops on the same piece of land simultaneously, is beneficial mainly because it
options: requires no consideration of compatible crop combinations
eliminates the need for weeding
maximises the use of land, light, and nutrients, and can reduce pest/disease spread
always doubles the yield of each individual crop
questions.explanation: Intercropping compatible crops (e.g., maize with legumes) makes efficient use of available space, light, and soil nutrients, and can help disrupt pest and disease cycles.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Mixed cropping differs from mixed farming in that mixed cropping involves
options: growing more than one crop on the same land at the same time, without livestock
keeping only one type of livestock
growing only a single crop species
rearing livestock together with crop production on the same farm
questions.explanation: Mixed cropping refers strictly to combining multiple crop species on the same land, while mixed farming combines both crop production and livestock rearing on the same farm.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The best time to harvest a cereal crop like maize is generally when the
options: grains have reached physiological maturity and moisture content has dropped sufficiently
plant is still flowering
field has just been irrigated
seedlings have just emerged
questions.explanation: Harvesting at physiological maturity, once grain moisture content has dropped to an appropriate level, minimises losses and ensures good storage quality.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which factor is most important in determining the appropriate spacing between crop plants during planting?
options: The colour of the crop's flowers
The nationality of the farmer
The growth habit and mature size of the crop
The time of day planting is done
questions.explanation: Plant spacing is determined by how large and how the crop grows (e.g., spreading vs. upright), ensuring adequate access to light, water, and nutrients without overcrowding.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Farm animals are broadly classified based on their digestive system into
options: male and female only
large and small animals only
domestic and wild animals only
ruminants and non-ruminants
questions.explanation: A key classification in animal husbandry distinguishes ruminants (e.g., cattle, goats, with a four-chambered stomach) from non-ruminants (e.g., pigs, poultry, with a simple stomach).

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Ruminant animals, such as cattle, are able to digest fibrous plant material efficiently mainly due to
options: chewing food only once before swallowing
microbial fermentation in their specialised, multi-chambered stomach (notably the rumen)
having exceptionally long intestines only
producing large amounts of saliva alone
questions.explanation: The rumen houses microorganisms that ferment and break down cellulose in plant fibre, a process non-ruminant animals cannot perform as efficiently.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The reproductive organ in the female mammal where fertilisation of the egg typically occurs is the
options: ovary
uterus
oviduct (fallopian tube)
vagina
questions.explanation: In mammals, sperm typically meets and fertilises the egg within the oviduct before the resulting zygote moves to the uterus for implantation and development.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Colostrum, the first milk produced by a mammal after giving birth, is especially important for the newborn because it
options: is rich in antibodies that provide passive immunity against disease
is identical in composition to regular milk
contains no nutritional value
is toxic and should be avoided
questions.explanation: Colostrum contains high concentrations of maternal antibodies, giving the newborn crucial passive immunity before its own immune system fully develops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A balanced livestock ration should supply which combination of nutrients?
options: Carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, and water in appropriate proportions
Only carbohydrates in large quantities
Only minerals and vitamins
Only protein and water
questions.explanation: A properly balanced ration supplies all essential nutrient classes in the correct proportions needed for the animal's growth, maintenance, and production needs.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a major function of protein in livestock nutrition?
options: Growth and repair of body tissues
Providing the main source of energy under normal conditions
Regulating body temperature directly
Insulating the body against cold
questions.explanation: Protein supplies amino acids essential for building and repairing muscle and other body tissues, distinct from carbohydrates and fats, which serve mainly as energy sources.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In poultry management, the practice of providing artificial heat to day-old chicks is called
options: vaccination
culling
brooding
debeaking
questions.explanation: Brooding provides supplementary heat (via a brooder) to young chicks that cannot yet regulate their own body temperature, crucial for their survival in early weeks.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Debeaking in poultry management is carried out mainly to
options: increase egg production directly
prevent diseases transmitted through water
prevent injurious pecking and cannibalism among birds
improve the taste of poultry meat
questions.explanation: Debeaking (trimming part of the beak) reduces the damage caused by pecking behaviour and cannibalism, which can occur especially in crowded poultry housing.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Culling in livestock management refers to the
options: process of feeding animals a balanced diet
vaccination of animals against disease
breeding of animals for desirable traits
removal of unproductive, sick, or undesirable animals from the herd or flock
questions.explanation: Culling improves overall herd/flock quality and productivity by systematically removing animals that are unproductive, diseased, or otherwise undesirable for breeding or production.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a common ectoparasite affecting cattle?
options: Tapeworm
Liver fluke (as an adult, found internally)
Roundworm
Tick
questions.explanation: Ticks attach to the external body surface of cattle, feeding on blood, making them ectoparasites, unlike internal (endo-) parasites such as roundworms and tapeworms.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Foot and mouth disease, a highly contagious viral disease, primarily affects
options: poultry exclusively
only animals with a single-toed hoof, like horses
fish only
cloven-hoofed animals such as cattle, sheep, and goats
questions.explanation: Foot and mouth disease specifically affects cloven-hoofed livestock, causing blisters on the mouth and feet, and is of major economic concern in cattle, sheep, and goats.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Newcastle disease is a major viral disease affecting
options: poultry
pigs
cattle
fish
questions.explanation: Newcastle disease is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease specifically affecting domestic and wild birds, particularly devastating in poultry flocks.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Vaccination of livestock is carried out mainly to
options: stimulate the animal's immune system to protect it against specific diseases
increase the animal's body weight directly
provide the animal with essential nutrients
improve the taste of the animal's meat
questions.explanation: Vaccines expose the immune system to a harmless form of a pathogen, triggering an immune response that provides protection against future infection by that disease.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Aquaculture refers to the
options: processing of fish into canned products only
capture of wild fish from open oceans
study of ocean currents
controlled cultivation and farming of fish and other aquatic organisms
questions.explanation: Aquaculture involves the deliberate breeding, rearing, and harvesting of fish and other aquatic organisms under controlled conditions, distinct from capture fisheries in the wild.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A fish pond used in aquaculture should ideally have which characteristic for good fish growth?
options: Adequate depth, good water quality, and sufficient dissolved oxygen
Very high salt concentration regardless of fish species
Completely stagnant water with no aeration
No access to sunlight at all
questions.explanation: Successful fish farming requires ponds with appropriate depth, clean water free of harmful pollutants, and sufficient dissolved oxygen to support healthy fish growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a major breed of cattle commonly reared in Nigeria for both milk and meat?
options: White Fulani
Yorkshire
Rhode Island Red
Large White
questions.explanation: White Fulani is a well-known indigenous Nigerian cattle breed valued as a dual-purpose breed for both milk and meat production.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a common breed of pig reared for pork production?
options: Large White
White Fulani
West African Dwarf
Rhode Island Red
questions.explanation: The Large White is a well-known commercial pig breed valued for its fast growth rate and lean meat production.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Farm animal housing is important mainly because it
options: replaces the need for veterinary care
guarantees higher market prices for produce
eliminates the need for feeding entirely
protects animals from adverse weather, predators, and helps in disease control
questions.explanation: Proper housing shields livestock from harsh weather and predators while also making it easier to manage feeding, hygiene, and disease prevention.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The gestation period is best defined as the
options: period an animal spends being weaned
time taken for an egg to be laid
period between hatching and maturity in birds
duration of pregnancy from conception to birth in a mammal
questions.explanation: Gestation period refers specifically to the length of pregnancy in mammals, varying by species (e.g., about 280 days in cattle, 114 days in pigs).

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a common method of livestock identification used on farms?
options: Ear tagging
Brooding
Debeaking
Culling
questions.explanation: Ear tagging attaches a numbered or coded tag to an animal's ear, allowing individual animals to be identified and tracked for breeding, health, and production records.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The factors of production in agriculture typically include
options: only land and labour
land, labour, capital, and management
only capital and machinery
only government subsidies
questions.explanation: As with general economics, agricultural production depends on land (natural resources), labour (human effort), capital (funds/equipment), and management/entrepreneurship to combine them efficiently.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Land, as a factor of agricultural production, is unique in that it is
options: the only factor required for production
easily created in unlimited amounts
fixed in supply and cannot be increased in total quantity
identical in quality and fertility everywhere
questions.explanation: Unlike capital or labour, the total physical quantity of land is fixed, though its productivity can be improved through better management practices.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A land tenure system refers to the
options: method of measuring the size of a farm
process of preparing land for planting
type of crop grown on a particular piece of land
set of rules and customs governing the ownership, use, and transfer of land
questions.explanation: Land tenure systems define how land rights are allocated, held, and transferred within a society, significantly influencing farmers' access to land for agricultural use.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The Land Use Act in Nigeria was enacted mainly to
options: transfer all farmland to the federal government directly
abolish all forms of private land ownership permanently
vest the ownership and control of land in state governments, held in trust for the people
prevent any form of land use for agriculture
questions.explanation: The Land Use Act of 1978 vested all land in each state in the governor, to be held in trust and administered for the common benefit of the people, affecting land access for farming.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agricultural credit refers to
options: funds borrowed by farmers to finance their farming activities
government taxes collected from farmers
the price paid by consumers for farm produce
the total value of a farmer's harvested produce
questions.explanation: Agricultural credit provides farmers with the necessary capital, often borrowed from banks or cooperatives, to purchase inputs and finance production before returns from sales come in.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agricultural marketing involves all activities related to the
options: application of fertiliser to farmland
actual cultivation of crops on the farm
breeding of improved livestock varieties
movement of farm produce from the point of production to the final consumer
questions.explanation: Agricultural marketing covers the full chain of assembling, grading, transporting, storing, and selling farm produce until it reaches the final consumer.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Farm records are important mainly because they help the farmer to
options: eliminate the need for farm labour
monitor farm performance, costs, and profitability over time
avoid the need for any government regulation
guarantee immunity from crop failure
questions.explanation: Keeping accurate farm records allows a farmer to track income, expenses, yields, and other key indicators, supporting better decision-making and financial planning.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Farm accounting specifically involves the
options: application of pesticides to control pests
breeding selection of superior livestock
physical planting and harvesting of crops
systematic recording and analysis of a farm's financial transactions
questions.explanation: Farm accounting focuses on tracking income, expenditure, assets, and liabilities of the farm business, essential for assessing profitability and planning.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the role of agricultural extension agents?
options: Manufacturing farm machinery and equipment
Collecting taxes from farmers on behalf of government
Educating farmers on improved practices and linking them with research findings
Setting the market price of agricultural produce
questions.explanation: Extension agents serve as a vital link between agricultural research institutions and farmers, teaching improved techniques and helping farmers adopt beneficial innovations.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cooperative societies in agriculture mainly benefit farmers by
options: guaranteeing fixed government-set prices for all produce
eliminating all competition among farmers permanently
pooling resources for better access to credit, inputs, and markets
replacing the need for individual farm management
questions.explanation: Agricultural cooperatives allow farmers to combine resources and bargaining power, improving access to credit, farm inputs, machinery, and better market prices.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Capital, as a factor of agricultural production, refers to
options: the entrepreneurial skill of the farm manager
man-made resources such as money, machinery, and buildings used in farming
the natural fertility of the soil
the physical effort provided by farm workers
questions.explanation: Capital represents man-made inputs (funds, tools, equipment, buildings) used alongside land and labour to carry out agricultural production.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The reward for the use of capital as a factor of production is called
options: profit
rent
wages
interest
questions.explanation: In economics, each factor of production earns a specific reward: land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest, and entrepreneurship/management earns profit.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The reward for the use of land as a factor of production is called
options: rent
interest
wages
profit
questions.explanation: Rent is the payment made for the use of land, distinguishing it from interest (reward for capital) and wages (reward for labour).

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The role of the entrepreneur (farm manager) in agricultural production is mainly to
options: provide only the physical machinery used
perform all manual labour on the farm personally
own all the land used in production
organise and combine the other factors of production and bear the risk of the enterprise
questions.explanation: The entrepreneur coordinates land, labour, and capital into productive use, making key decisions and bearing the financial risk of the farming enterprise, earning profit as a reward.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agriculture is often described as a science, an art, and a business because it involves
options: only the manual labour of farmers with no scientific input
the application of scientific knowledge, practical skills, and profit-oriented management
government regulation alone with no farmer involvement
purely theoretical study with no practical application
questions.explanation: Agriculture applies scientific principles (science), requires practical skill in carrying out operations (art), and is managed to achieve profit like any enterprise (business).

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agricultural engineering, as a branch of agriculture, is mainly concerned with
options: the marketing of farm produce
the design and application of machinery, structures, and equipment used in farming
the study of farm animal diseases
the breeding of improved crop varieties
questions.explanation: Agricultural engineering applies engineering principles to farm machinery, irrigation systems, farm structures, and processing equipment, distinct from agronomy or animal science.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: One major importance of agriculture in rural communities is that it
options: discourages the growth of rural markets
is practised only by people with university education
eliminates the need for any form of rural infrastructure
provides employment and a source of livelihood for the majority of rural dwellers
questions.explanation: Agriculture remains the dominant occupation and source of income for most rural populations in developing countries such as Nigeria.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In agricultural ecology, biotic factors are best described as
options: non-living components such as temperature and rainfall
living components of the environment, such as plants, animals, and micro-organisms, that affect crop and livestock production
man-made structures found on the farm
the chemical composition of farm soil only
questions.explanation: Biotic factors are the living organisms in an ecosystem, including pests, weeds, pollinators, and micro-organisms, that interact with and influence crops and livestock.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Abiotic factors in an agricultural ecosystem refer to
options: the farmer's management decisions
non-living physical and chemical components such as temperature, rainfall, and soil minerals
living organisms such as pests and weeds
market prices of farm produce
questions.explanation: Abiotic factors are the non-living elements of the environment, including climate and soil properties, that influence the growth and distribution of crops and livestock.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Mitosis, a type of cell division important in living organisms, mainly results in
options: two daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell, enabling growth and repair
four daughter cells with half the chromosome number of the parent cell
the formation of gametes for sexual reproduction
the permanent fusion of two separate cells
questions.explanation: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells from one parent cell, the basis for growth, tissue repair, and asexual reproduction in organisms.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Meiosis is a type of cell division that is important mainly because it
options: produces gametes with half the chromosome number, maintaining a constant chromosome number across generations
occurs only in plant root tips
produces cells identical to the parent cell for tissue growth
combines two separate organisms into one
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number during gamete formation, so that when two gametes fuse at fertilisation, the normal chromosome number is restored in the offspring.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Mendel's law of segregation states that
options: the two alleles for a trait separate from each other during gamete formation, with each gamete receiving only one allele
dominant alleles are always destroyed during meiosis
different genes for different traits always assort independently of each other
all offspring must show a blend of both parents' traits
questions.explanation: Mendel's law of segregation explains that paired alleles separate during meiosis so each gamete carries only one allele of a gene pair, later reunited at fertilisation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In a genetic cross, a dominant allele is one that
options: never appears in the offspring of a cross
is always inherited from the mother only
expresses its trait in the phenotype whenever it is present, masking the recessive allele
is only expressed when paired with another dominant allele
questions.explanation: A dominant allele produces its phenotypic effect even in the heterozygous state, masking the effect of the recessive allele on the other chromosome.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous parents (Aa x Aa), the expected phenotypic ratio of offspring is
options: 3 dominant : 1 recessive
9 dominant : 3 recessive
1 dominant : 3 recessive
1 dominant : 1 recessive
questions.explanation: Crossing two heterozygous individuals for a single gene (Aa x Aa) typically produces offspring in a 3:1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In a dihybrid cross between two individuals heterozygous for two independently assorting genes, the expected phenotypic ratio of offspring is
questions.explanation: A dihybrid cross (AaBb x AaBb) involving two independently assorting gene pairs typically yields offspring in the classic 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The genotype of an organism refers to its
options: genetic constitution, that is, the actual alleles it carries for a trait
total body weight at maturity
outward, observable physical appearance
geographic location of origin
questions.explanation: Genotype describes the specific alleles an organism possesses for a given gene, while phenotype describes the observable expression of those genes.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Certified seeds are considered a superior farm input mainly because they
options: can be planted at any time of the year regardless of climate
require no soil preparation before planting
are guaranteed to be genetically pure, high-yielding, and free from disease and weed contamination
are always cheaper than uncertified seeds
questions.explanation: Certified seeds are produced and inspected under quality control standards, ensuring genetic purity, high germination rate, and freedom from seed-borne diseases and weeds.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agrochemicals, as farm inputs, include products such as
options: farm buildings and storage silos
seeds and planting materials only
fertilisers, herbicides, and insecticides used to boost yield and control pests
tractors and ploughs used for tillage
questions.explanation: Agrochemicals are manufactured chemical inputs, such as fertilisers and pesticides, used to supply nutrients or control pests, weeds, and diseases in crop production.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The Operation Feed the Nation programme, launched by the Nigerian government, was aimed primarily at
options: banning the importation of all agricultural machinery
establishing private commercial banks across the country
encouraging citizens to engage in food production to achieve national food self-sufficiency
regulating the price of imported manufactured goods
questions.explanation: Operation Feed the Nation was a national programme launched to mobilise citizens toward increased food crop production and reduce dependence on food imports.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The FADAMA programme in Nigeria was primarily established to
options: improve rural livelihoods by developing irrigation and providing support for farmers along floodplain areas
regulate the exportation of cash crops only
construct urban housing estates
provide scholarships for agricultural students abroad
questions.explanation: FADAMA is a World Bank-assisted programme that supports farmers in floodplain (fadama) areas through irrigation infrastructure, inputs, and rural livelihood improvement.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) contribute to agricultural development mainly by
options: printing the country's currency for agricultural trade
providing training, funding, and technical support to farmers, often in underserved areas
setting national import and export tariffs
enforcing land tenure laws in rural communities
questions.explanation: NGOs often complement government efforts by offering farmer training, micro-credit, and technical assistance, particularly in rural or underserved agricultural communities.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The Green Revolution refers to a period of agricultural reform mainly aimed at
options: converting farmland into industrial estates
increasing crop yields through improved varieties, fertiliser use, and irrigation
banning the use of any modern farm inputs
reducing the amount of land available for cultivation
questions.explanation: The Green Revolution promoted high-yielding crop varieties combined with fertilisers, irrigation, and mechanisation to substantially raise agricultural productivity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Igneous rock, one of the major parent materials from which soil is formed, originates from
options: the compression of layers of sediment over time
the alteration of existing rock by heat and pressure
the cooling and solidification of molten magma or lava
the decomposition of plant and animal remains
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks, such as granite and basalt, form when molten magma or lava cools and solidifies, and they serve as an important parent material for soil formation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Physical weathering differs from chemical weathering of rocks in that physical weathering involves
options: the addition of organic matter to weathered rock
the action of living organisms only
a change in the chemical composition of the rock through reactions such as oxidation
the mechanical breakdown of rock into smaller particles without changing its chemical composition
questions.explanation: Physical (mechanical) weathering breaks rocks into smaller fragments through processes like temperature changes and frost action, without altering their chemical make-up, unlike chemical weathering.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Gravitational water in the soil is best described as water that
options: moves freely downward through the large soil pores under the pull of gravity
is tightly bound to soil particles and unavailable to plants
is held permanently in the smallest soil pores
exists only as water vapour in soil air spaces
questions.explanation: Gravitational water drains freely through the larger soil pores due to gravity and is generally not retained long enough to be fully utilised by plant roots.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Hygroscopic water in the soil refers to water that is
options: tightly held as a thin film around soil particles and largely unavailable for plant uptake
the main source of water absorbed by plant roots
found only in waterlogged soils
freely draining through large pore spaces under gravity
questions.explanation: Hygroscopic water is held so tightly by adhesive forces around soil particles that it is essentially unavailable to plants, unlike the more available capillary water.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Field capacity refers to the amount of water
options: remaining in the soil after excess gravitational water has drained away
present in the soil immediately after a rainfall event
required to saturate the entire soil profile permanently
lost from the soil through evaporation alone
questions.explanation: Field capacity is the water content of soil after free drainage of gravitational water has stopped, representing the maximum water available for plant use.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The permanent wilting point of soil is the moisture level at which
options: soil is completely saturated with water
soil nutrients become most available to plants
plants can no longer extract sufficient water and remain wilted even after watering
gravitational water begins to drain rapidly
questions.explanation: At the permanent wilting point, the remaining soil water is held so tightly that plant roots cannot extract it, causing the plant to remain wilted even under favourable conditions.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Contour ploughing, a soil conservation practice, helps to control erosion mainly by
options: removing all vegetation cover from sloping land
creating furrows across the slope that slow down and trap surface run-off
increasing the speed of water flow down a slope
compacting the soil to prevent water infiltration entirely
questions.explanation: Ploughing along the natural contour of a slope, rather than up and down it, creates ridges that slow run-off and reduce soil loss on hilly farmland.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Terracing, as a method of soil erosion control, involves
options: removing topsoil completely from hilly land
planting a single crop species across a whole hillside
constructing a series of levelled platforms on a slope to reduce the speed of water run-off
digging deep vertical channels down a slope
questions.explanation: Terracing transforms a steep slope into a series of flat steps, reducing the velocity of run-off and thereby minimising soil erosion on hilly terrain.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cover cropping is a soil conservation practice that mainly helps to
options: protect the soil surface from the direct impact of rain and reduce erosion
prevent any organic matter from entering the soil
eliminate the need for crop rotation permanently
increase the rate of soil erosion on bare land
questions.explanation: Cover crops shield the soil surface from the direct impact of raindrops and wind, reducing splash erosion and run-off while often adding organic matter.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In the carbon cycle, green plants remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere mainly through the process of
options: photosynthesis
combustion
decomposition
respiration
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants absorb atmospheric carbon dioxide and convert it, using sunlight, into organic compounds such as glucose.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Carbon dioxide is returned to the atmosphere in the carbon cycle mainly through processes such as
options: photosynthesis in green plants
nitrogen fixation by root nodule bacteria
respiration of living organisms and decomposition of organic matter
absorption of nitrates by plant roots
questions.explanation: Respiration by plants and animals, along with the decomposition of dead organic matter by micro-organisms, releases carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere, completing the carbon cycle.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Phosphorus is an essential plant nutrient mainly important for
options: increasing the water content of the soil
the formation of chlorophyll and leafy growth
root development and flowering/fruiting
controlling soil pH directly
questions.explanation: Phosphorus promotes strong root development, and flowering and fruit formation, whereas nitrogen is primarily linked to vegetative (leafy) growth and chlorophyll formation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Potassium, an essential macronutrient, is important in plants mainly for
options: primarily driving chlorophyll formation
improving disease resistance and the overall quality and strength of plant tissue
fixing atmospheric nitrogen in the soil
forming the bulk of plant proteins
questions.explanation: Potassium strengthens plant tissues, improves resistance to disease and lodging, and regulates water balance within the plant, distinct from nitrogen's role in vegetative growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Macronutrients differ from micronutrients in plant nutrition in that macronutrients are required
options: in relatively large quantities, such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium
exclusively by animals and not by plants
only during the seedling stage of a plant's life
only in trace amounts, such as zinc and boron
questions.explanation: Macronutrients (e.g., nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) are needed by plants in large amounts, while micronutrients (e.g., zinc, boron, iron) are needed only in trace quantities.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Compost is prepared mainly by
options: storing fresh animal dung without any decomposition
burning crop residues completely to ash
mixing inorganic fertilisers with water
allowing plant and animal waste to decompose under controlled conditions into a nutrient-rich manure
questions.explanation: Composting is the controlled decomposition of organic materials such as crop residues and animal waste, producing a nutrient-rich organic manure for soil improvement.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Green manuring involves the practice of
options: spraying green-coloured pesticides on crops
harvesting mature crops for animal feed
ploughing young, green plants directly into the soil to decompose and improve fertility
applying only inorganic fertiliser to growing crops
questions.explanation: Green manuring incorporates fresh, green plant material (often legumes) directly into the soil, where it decomposes and enriches the soil with organic matter and nutrients.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Broadcasting, as a method of planting, involves
options: placing seeds individually in holes at fixed spacing
transplanting seedlings from a nursery bed
scattering seeds randomly and evenly over the entire prepared seedbed
sowing seeds in continuous rows using a drill
questions.explanation: Broadcasting scatters seeds by hand or machine over the whole field surface, commonly used for crops like rice and some pasture grasses, unlike row planting or dibbling.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Seed dormancy refers to a condition in which a viable seed
options: fails to germinate even under favourable environmental conditions until the dormancy is broken
loses its ability to ever germinate
requires no water at all to germinate
germinates immediately regardless of environmental conditions
questions.explanation: A dormant seed is alive and viable but will not germinate until specific internal or external conditions, such as scarification or after-ripening, allow dormancy to be broken.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Propagation of plants using stem cuttings is an example of
options: sexual propagation through seeds
vegetative (asexual) propagation
propagation through spores only
propagation using pollen grains
questions.explanation: Using stem cuttings to grow new plants is a form of vegetative propagation, producing genetically identical plants without the use of seeds or fertilisation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Weevils are a major concern in the storage of cereal grains mainly because they
options: bore into and feed on stored grains, causing significant post-harvest losses
improve the germination rate of stored seeds
prevent fungal growth in grain stores
add nutritional value to stored grains
questions.explanation: Weevils are common storage pests that bore into grains such as maize and rice, causing considerable quantity and quality losses if not properly controlled.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A traditional crib used for storing maize is designed mainly to
options: cook the maize while in storage
keep maize permanently wet for easier processing
prevent any air from reaching the stored grain
allow good ventilation and reduce moisture, thereby preventing mould and pest damage
questions.explanation: Cribs are raised, well-ventilated structures that allow air to circulate through the stored maize cobs, reducing moisture content and limiting mould and pest infestation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The gizzard in the digestive system of poultry functions mainly to
options: grind and break down food, often with the help of small stones (grit)
absorb digested nutrients into the bloodstream
produce digestive enzymes for protein breakdown
temporarily store food before digestion
questions.explanation: The muscular gizzard grinds food, often aided by ingested grit, compensating for the bird's lack of teeth and preparing food for further digestion.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In the stomach of a ruminant such as cattle, the four compartments in the correct order that food passes through are the
options: rumen, reticulum, omasum, and abomasum
abomasum, omasum, reticulum, and rumen
reticulum, abomasum, rumen, and omasum
omasum, rumen, abomasum, and reticulum
questions.explanation: Ingested feed passes sequentially through the rumen (fermentation), reticulum (further breakdown and cud formation), omasum (water absorption), and finally the abomasum (true glandular stomach).

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Air sacs, found in the respiratory system of birds, function mainly to
options: produce eggs within the reproductive tract
regulate the bird's body temperature through sweating
store air and improve the efficiency of gas exchange in the lungs
digest food more efficiently
questions.explanation: Air sacs act as bellows that push air continuously through the lungs, allowing for a highly efficient, one-way flow of air that supports the high metabolic demands of flight and growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The testes in the male reproductive system of livestock are primarily responsible for
options: storing fertilised eggs during pregnancy
producing eggs (ova) for reproduction
producing milk for offspring
producing sperm cells and the male hormone testosterone
questions.explanation: The testes are the primary male reproductive organs, producing both sperm cells through spermatogenesis and testosterone, the principal male sex hormone.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The oestrus cycle in female livestock refers to the
options: process by which milk is produced after birth
stage at which an animal is weaned from its mother
period during which an animal is exclusively pregnant
recurring series of physiological changes associated with reproduction, including the period of sexual receptivity (heat)
questions.explanation: The oestrus cycle describes the recurring reproductive cycle in female mammals, including the period of heat (oestrus) when the female is receptive to mating.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Artificial insemination is a livestock breeding technique valued mainly because it allows
options: widespread use of semen from genetically superior males without the need for natural mating
farmers to avoid feeding their breeding animals
elimination of all inherited diseases automatically
animals to reproduce without any reproductive organs
questions.explanation: Artificial insemination allows semen from a single genetically superior sire to be used to breed many females across different locations, improving herd genetics without natural mating.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A deficiency of Vitamin A in livestock commonly results in
options: improved reproductive performance
soft, brittle bones and rickets
night blindness and poor growth
excessive weight gain
questions.explanation: Vitamin A is essential for vision and epithelial tissue health, so its deficiency commonly causes night blindness, poor growth, and increased susceptibility to infection in livestock.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A deficiency of calcium in laying hens commonly results in
options: thin or soft-shelled eggs and weakened bones
increased fertility of eggs
improved feather quality
faster growth rate in chicks
questions.explanation: Calcium is essential for eggshell formation and skeletal strength, so a deficiency in laying hens leads to soft or thin-shelled eggs and weakened bone structure.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The Pearson square method is a technique commonly used in animal nutrition to
options: diagnose parasitic infections in livestock
determine the age of an animal from its teeth
calculate the proportions of two feed ingredients needed to achieve a desired nutrient level in a ration
measure the body weight of livestock
questions.explanation: The Pearson square is a simple mathematical method used to calculate the correct proportions of two or more feed ingredients required to formulate a ration with a target nutrient content.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Roughages differ from concentrates in livestock feeds in that roughages
options: can only be fed to poultry and not to ruminants
are low in fibre but very high in energy and protein content
must always be provided in powdered form
are bulky feeds with high fibre content and relatively low nutrient density
questions.explanation: Roughages, such as hay and grass, are bulky and high in fibre but comparatively low in energy and protein, while concentrates are nutrient-dense with low fibre content.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Silage is prepared mainly by
options: storing green, chopped forage under anaerobic conditions to ferment and preserve it for feeding
drying green forage completely under the sun before storage
grinding dry grains into a fine powder
boiling forage crops before feeding to livestock
questions.explanation: Silage making preserves green fodder by packing it tightly to exclude air, allowing controlled fermentation that maintains its nutritional value for later feeding, especially in the dry season.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Hay making, a method of preserving forage, mainly involves
options: boiling green forage to kill harmful bacteria
cutting and sun-drying green forage to a low moisture content for storage
fermenting green forage in an airtight container
freezing green forage for long-term storage
questions.explanation: Hay is made by cutting forage at the right growth stage and drying it under the sun until its moisture content is low enough to prevent spoilage during storage.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The deep litter system of poultry housing involves
options: housing birds exclusively in underground pits
confining each bird individually in a small elevated wire cage
allowing birds to roam freely without any form of housing
keeping birds on a floor covered with absorbent material such as wood shavings or straw
questions.explanation: In the deep litter system, birds are raised on the floor of a house covered with litter material like wood shavings, which absorbs droppings and provides a comfortable surface.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The battery cage system of poultry housing is characterised mainly by
options: allowing birds unrestricted access to open pasture
housing birds on a floor with deep litter material
keeping birds in individual wire cages, often arranged in tiers, to ease management and egg collection
keeping birds exclusively outdoors without shelter
questions.explanation: The battery cage system confines individual birds (mainly layers) in wire cages stacked in tiers, simplifying feeding, egg collection, and disease control, though it limits movement.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Disinfection of livestock housing and equipment is carried out mainly to
options: improve the genetic quality of the herd
increase the nutritional value of animal feed
reduce the labour required for feeding animals
destroy disease-causing organisms and reduce the risk of infection
questions.explanation: Disinfection uses chemical agents to kill pathogenic micro-organisms on surfaces and equipment, reducing disease transmission risk within a livestock facility.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Liver fluke is classified as an endoparasite of livestock mainly because it
options: lives and feeds inside the body of its host, particularly the liver and bile ducts
attaches to and feeds on the external skin surface of the host
is a type of bacteria rather than a parasitic worm
lives freely in the soil without any host
questions.explanation: Liver fluke is an internal (endo-) parasite that resides within the liver and bile ducts of its host, unlike ectoparasites such as ticks that live on the outer body surface.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Coccidiosis, a common disease of poultry caused by a protozoan parasite, mainly affects the
options: intestinal lining, causing bloody diarrhoea and poor growth
skeletal system, causing brittle bones
respiratory system, causing severe coughing
reproductive system, causing complete infertility
questions.explanation: Coccidiosis is caused by protozoan parasites that damage the intestinal lining of birds, resulting in bloody diarrhoea, poor feed conversion, and reduced growth or death if untreated.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Mastitis, a common disease in dairy cattle, is characterised mainly by
options: inflammation of the respiratory tract
swelling of the joints, causing lameness
inflammation of the udder, often reducing milk yield and quality
loss of appetite with no other symptoms
questions.explanation: Mastitis is an inflammation of the mammary gland (udder), usually caused by bacterial infection, leading to reduced milk yield and altered milk quality in dairy cattle.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Trypanosomiasis, a serious disease of cattle in tropical Africa, is transmitted mainly by the bite of the
options: tick
housefly
tsetse fly
mosquito
questions.explanation: Trypanosomiasis (nagana) is caused by trypanosome parasites transmitted through the bite of the tsetse fly, significantly limiting cattle rearing in tsetse-infested regions of Africa.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a common system used for rearing fish in aquaculture?
options: Deep litter houses on dry land
Earthen ponds, concrete tanks, and floating cages
Underground burrows dug by the farmer
Battery cages suspended in the air
questions.explanation: Fish are commonly reared in earthen ponds, concrete or plastic tanks, or floating/fixed cages placed in larger water bodies, each system suited to different scales of production.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Smoking, as a method of fish processing, is used mainly to
options: kill the fish before it can be harvested
increase the moisture content of fresh fish
add colour to fish without affecting its shelf life
reduce moisture content and preserve fish for a longer shelf life
questions.explanation: Smoking dehydrates fish and deposits preservative compounds from the smoke, inhibiting microbial growth and significantly extending the fish's shelf life.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Apiculture, the practice of bee-keeping, is valued mainly for the production of
options: honey and beeswax
wool and hide
milk and meat
eggs and feathers
questions.explanation: Apiculture focuses on rearing honeybee colonies primarily to harvest honey and beeswax, along with benefits like pollination of crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A typical honeybee colony is organised into three main castes, namely
options: the queen, larvae, and pupae only
the queen, worker bees, and drones
male bees, female bees, and eggs
workers, eggs, and honeycombs
questions.explanation: A honeybee colony consists of a single reproductive queen, numerous sterile female worker bees that perform colony tasks, and male drones whose main role is to mate with a queen.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Weaning in livestock management refers to the
options: process of introducing a bull to a herd of cows
gradual withdrawal of young animals from dependence on their mother's milk to solid feed
vaccination of young animals against disease
removal of horns from young cattle
